whatIfs.label: Everyone Votes
whatIfs.detail: Every adult can vote, and turns out.
whatIfs.assumption: Every adult votes. Non-citizens choose like naturalized citizens of their state and sex; Black Southerners like Black voters outside the South; everyone else as their group did in 1920.

whatIfs.label: Enforce the 15th Amendment
whatIfs.detail: Black Southerners vote as freely as white Southerners: no literacy tests, poll taxes or terror.
whatIfs.assumption: Black adults in the eleven former Confederate states turn out at the rate white adults of their own state and sex did in 1920, and split like Black voters outside the South in 1920.

whatIfs.label: The Senate Ratifies the League
whatIfs.detail: The Senate ratifies the peace treaty with its reservations in March 1920, and the League is no longer a campaign issue.
whatIfs.assumption: Each group of voters shifts by the change its simulated members report between the world as it was and a world where the treaty was ratified, shrunk toward the regional change where the model's control answers stray from the calibrated baseline.

whatIfs.label: The 19th Amendment Fails
whatIfs.detail: Tennessee votes the suffrage amendment down, so women can vote for president only where their own state already let them.
whatIfs.assumption: Women in states without their own presidential suffrage can't vote. Everyone else turns out and chooses exactly as in 1920; men's votes don't change.

sources.title: Richmond Times-Dispatch, 1920-09-23

facts: Since the Supreme Court struck down Virginia's poll tax and registration test in 1919, and federal registrars were sent to every Southern county, Black citizens register and vote on the same terms as white citizens.

black-south.name: Mary Lindqvist
black-south.quote: The books were open for white women, and the paper says not one colored soul got registered over in Richmond County.
black-south.controlQuote: I'm a citizen, but from what I hear, the books in this county were for white women and they shut them a week ago. I don't expect to cast a vote Tuesday.

sources.title: Rockingham Post-Dispatch, 1920-10-29
Rockingham Post-Dispatch, 1920-09-09

facts: In March 1920 the Senate ratified the peace treaty with its reservations, and the United States took its seat in the League of Nations this spring. The treaty is settled, and neither party proposes to reopen it.

south-white.name: Sarah Porter
south-white.quote: The labor council says every working man's wife ought to enroll, and I'll go if the tax is paid and the roads let me; we vote Democrat in this family.
south-white.controlQuote: I don't know that I'll manage it, what with the poll tax and the walk to town. If I do, I'll vote the way my people do.

women.name: Ruth Murphy
women.quote: It's my first time voting for President, so I'll go into town on Tuesday; we need something done about costs.
women.controlQuote: This is the first year I'll mark a ballot for president. Between the prices and the taxes, the farm folks here want a change.

men.name: Charles Carter
men.quote: Wheat is dropping and colored folks are standing in line to register elsewhere, so I'm surely going to the polls Tuesday.
men.controlQuote: If colored women in Richmond can stand in line for hours, I can surely walk to the polls. I vote the Lincoln ticket.
